Pregnancy

COVID-19 in pregnancy: understanding complications and research

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

COVID-19 can increase the risk of serious illness during pregnancy, but research percentages need careful interpretation. A widely reported study of 2020 births remains informative when its dates, outcome definitions and limits are kept visible.

The study behind the headline is historical

The NIH-funded research discussed here was published in JAMA in February 2022. It examined births from March through early December 2020, before COVID-19 vaccination was available. Calling it a new study without those dates would hide an important part of its meaning.

Researchers assessed 14,104 pregnant patients at seventeen hospitals in the United States; 2,352 had SARS-CoV-2 infection. They compared serious obstetric outcomes in those with and without a positive test and also examined differences by illness severity.

This was observational research, not an experiment assigning people to become infected. It helps identify associations and patterns, but it cannot supply an exact forecast for a particular pregnancy today. The circulating variants, prior immunity, available treatments and clinical setting have changed since the study period.

A composite outcome is not the same as one complication

The main outcome combined maternal death with serious problems related to pregnancy-associated hypertension, postpartum haemorrhage or an infection other than SARS-CoV-2. A patient experiencing any qualifying event could count toward that combined outcome.

In the overall comparison, it occurred in 13.4% of patients with infection and 9.2% of those without. The adjusted relative risk was 1.41. That does not mean that 13.4% died or that each individual complication increased by exactly the same amount.

Combining outcomes can help researchers study serious illness, but it makes careful reading essential. Ask what counted, whether results were adjusted for other differences and whether the number concerns the parent, the baby or both. A headline about complications often compresses several distinct outcomes into one phrase.

Severity changed the association

For the moderate-or-higher severity subgroup, the adjusted relative risk for the main composite was 2.06, not the overall 1.41. The subgroup therefore should not be described merely by copying the approximately forty-percent overall relative increase.

The study did not find a statistically significant increase in that primary outcome for mild or asymptomatic infection. This is narrower than saying mild infection can never affect a pregnancy. An absence of a statistically significant association for a particular outcome is not proof of zero risk in every setting.

Severity can also change after an initially mild start. A reassuring headline should not discourage you from contacting maternity care if symptoms worsen. Your team needs the current illness pattern and your pregnancy history, not only the label attached to the first day of infection.

Caesarean birth, premature birth and infant outcomes need separate reading

The report also considered delivery and infant outcomes. Moderate-or-higher illness was associated with more caesarean births, while preterm birth was another concern in the research. These are different endpoints from the main maternal composite and should not share one interchangeable percentage.

For fetal or neonatal death, the overall adjusted confidence interval included no association. That detail matters: a higher unadjusted percentage is not the same as a clearly demonstrated independent effect in the adjusted analysis. Nor does uncertainty in this one estimate show that the wider evidence about stillbirth can be ignored.

Current CDC guidance identifies increased risks of preterm birth and stillbirth across the broader evidence base. For an individual family, infection does not make those outcomes inevitable. Delivery timing and mode depend on the actual maternal and fetal situation, rather than a positive test automatically requiring a caesarean.

Relative risk is not a personal probability

A relative increase compares two groups. It is different from the absolute proportion of people who experienced an outcome. Saying a risk is higher does not mean that most people will have the complication, and a percentage increase should not be added directly to your chance of an uncomplicated birth.

Adjustment helps researchers account for measured differences between groups, but it cannot remove every difference in health, testing or care. The group without a positive test and the group with severe illness may differ in ways that affect outcomes independently of the virus.

Use the study to understand why clinicians take infection in pregnancy seriously. Do not use its numbers as a calculator for your own pregnancy. Your vaccination history, current symptoms, underlying conditions, stage of pregnancy and access to treatment all belong in the conversation.

Pregnancy changes the response to illness

Pregnancy involves changes in immune regulation, breathing and circulation. It is misleading to describe the immune system as simply switched off to protect the fetus. The body continues to defend against infection, while some infections can carry greater consequences during pregnancy.

Severe respiratory illness can interfere with oxygen delivery and place stress on several organs. Inflammation and changes involving blood vessels or clotting may also contribute to complications. Possible effects on the placenta have been investigated, but a proposed mechanism is not proof that it occurred in every pregnancy in a study.

The image of coronavirus merely coating the lungs in sticky material is too simplistic to guide care. A more useful explanation connects symptoms and clinical findings to the support needed. If you are unwell, the team may assess breathing, hydration and pregnancy-specific concerns together.

Other health conditions influence the care plan

Conditions such as obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure or significant immune suppression can add to concern about severe illness. The level of control, treatment and combination of conditions matter. A diagnosis alone should not be used to make an identical prediction for everyone who has it.

For example, HIV infection and severe immune suppression are not interchangeable descriptions. Tell your maternity and medical teams about your actual treatment and health status rather than assuming that a general list has already classified your risk.

Keep taking prescribed treatment unless your clinician advises a change, and ask early about symptoms or medicine interactions. If several teams look after you, make sure each knows you are pregnant and has the same medication list. Coordinated care is more useful than trying to compare your situation with someone else’s illness online.

Vaccination remains part of prevention

The 2020 cohort could not measure the effect of vaccination because vaccines were not yet available. Later vaccination evidence therefore needs to be considered separately from that study. CDC information describes protection against severe disease and reassuring pregnancy safety findings.

In March 2026, ACOG reaffirmed its recommendation for updated COVID-19 vaccination during pregnancy and related reproductive stages. National programmes can use different eligibility and decision-making frameworks, and seasonal formulations and schedules change. Check current local guidance with your maternity team rather than following an old article’s dose timetable.

Vaccination reduces risk; it cannot promise that infection or every pregnancy complication will be prevented. Discuss your previous doses, any prior reaction and when you last had COVID-19. That makes the prevention conversation specific to you without treating the historical study as a vaccine trial.

If you become unwell, ask about treatment promptly

Let your maternity team know about a positive test or symptoms suggestive of COVID-19, particularly if you have other health conditions. Describe when symptoms started, whether they are worsening and how you are managing food and fluids. Early contact helps the team decide whether treatment or assessment is appropriate.

Pregnancy or breastfeeding alone is not a reason to withhold COVID-19 treatment. A clinician should choose an option according to timing, illness severity, medicine interactions and kidney or liver considerations. Do not start another person’s medicine or assume every antiviral has the same instructions.

Keep routine pregnancy care coordinated while you are ill. If an appointment needs to change, call the service for a plan rather than simply missing it. Recovery from the acute infection does not mean that persistent breathing problems, unusual fatigue or other new symptoms must be ignored.

Know which symptoms need urgent help

Difficulty breathing, chest pain, fainting or becoming seriously unwell needs urgent or emergency assessment. Tell the service that you are pregnant or recently gave birth. Do not wait for a COVID test to turn positive before seeking help for severe symptoms.

Reduced or changed baby movements, significant bleeding, leaking fluid, severe abdominal pain or a persistent severe headache with visual changes also requires prompt maternity advice. These concerns may have causes other than COVID-19 and should not be dismissed as part of a viral illness.

Ask who to contact during the day and out of hours, what to monitor at home and when follow-up is needed. The practical message from the research is to prevent severe illness where possible and respond to symptoms early, while keeping historical group findings separate from predictions about your baby.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

The cited study used 2020 data, before vaccination.

Overall and severity-specific estimates answer different questions.

Current care should consider vaccination, treatment and the individual pregnancy.

How BeMama can help

Keep the symptom start date, medication list and maternity contact numbers together so you can get clear advice quickly if you become unwell.

When to seek help

Seek urgent help for breathing difficulty, chest pain, severe illness or urgent maternity symptoms such as reduced baby movements, significant bleeding or a severe persistent headache with visual changes.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A composite complication rate is not a death rate.
  • Mild illness was not a guarantee of zero risk.
  • Historical percentages cannot predict one pregnancy today.
  • Vaccination guidance and treatment decisions need current local context.
  • Do not delay care for urgent respiratory or maternity symptoms.

Frequently asked questions

Was this study conducted after vaccines became available?

No. It examined births in 2020, before vaccination, and was published in February 2022.

Does the 13.4% figure mean maternal death?

No. It describes a combined outcome including several serious obstetric complications and death.

Was the moderate-or-higher subgroup estimate 1.41?

No. Its adjusted relative risk was 2.06 for the primary composite; 1.41 was the overall estimate.

Does a non-significant result prove mild infection is harmless?

No. It concerns a particular study outcome and does not prove zero risk for every pregnancy.

Does a positive test automatically require a caesarean?

No. Delivery decisions depend on maternal and fetal circumstances.

Can I use the study percentage as my personal risk?

No. It is a historical group estimate, not an individual prediction.

Does pregnancy switch off the immune system?

No. Immune regulation changes, but the immune system continues to function.

Did the 2020 study test vaccine effectiveness?

No. Vaccination evidence comes from later research and should be considered separately.

Must COVID treatment be avoided during pregnancy?

No. Pregnancy alone is not a reason to withhold treatment; a clinician should select the appropriate option.

Should reduced baby movements wait until my infection clears?

No. Contact maternity care promptly; do not attribute a movement change to COVID-19 without assessment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
